Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 114, verses 1–6:

﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind﴾. If it is asked: why did He attribute the Lord (rabb) specifically to mankind, when He is the Lord of everything? The answer: the seeking of refuge was from the evil of the whisperer who whispers into the breasts of people. So He singled them out for mention, because they are the ones who seek protection with this formula, and they are the intended ones here, not others. ﴿The King of mankind, the God of mankind﴾. This is ʿatf bayan (explanatory apposition). If it is asked: why did He mention His attributes in the order Lord, then King, then God? The answer: this is in ascending order of rank. The term "lord" (rabb) may be applied to many people, as one says "so-and-so is the lord of the house" and the like, so it was mentioned first because its meaning is shared. As for "king" (malik), it is applied only to a certain category of people, the kings, and there is no doubt that they are higher than the rest of people. Therefore it came after "lord." As for "God" (ilah), He is higher than the king, which is why kings do not claim to be gods. The God is only One, without partner or equal, so the attributes were concluded with Him.

If it is asked: why did he repeat the explicit mention of the genitive "mankind" in the second and third instances, rather than using a pronoun in both, given that it was mentioned earlier in "Lord of mankind"? Or why was it not enough to mention it explicitly only the second time? The answer: since it was an explanatory apposition, explicitness was appropriate there, because explanation requires clarity rather than pronouns. It was also intended to give attention to the repeated term, as in the saying of the poet:

"I see nothing outrunning death; death humbles the rich man and the poor man alike."

﴿The whisperer﴾ (al-waswas). It is derived from waswasa, which is hidden speech. It may be that al-waswas carries the meaning of al-muwaswis (the one who whispers), as if it were an active participle. This appears from the statement of Ibn ʿAtiyya: "al-waswas is among the names of Satan." It may also be a verbal noun (masdar) used to describe the whisperer for emphasis, like ʿaddal and sawwam, or it may be by omission of a noun, its meaning being "the possessor of whispering" (dhi al-waswas). Al-Zamakhshari said: the verbal noun is actually waswas with bi-l-kufr (whispering of disbelief).

﴿The sneaking one (al-khannas)﴾. Its meaning is the one who retreats on his heels and recurs occasionally. This applies fully to Satan: he whispers, and when the servant remembers God and seeks refuge in Him, he withdraws from him. Then he returns to him at a time of heedlessness from remembrance. He sneaks back in his withdrawal and then in his return after that.

﴿Who whispers into the breasts of mankind﴾. Satan's whispering into the breast of a human being takes many forms. Among them: corrupting faith and casting doubt on beliefs. If he cannot do that, he orders him to commit sins. If he cannot do that, he discourages him from acts of obedience. If he cannot do that, he introduces showing-off (riya') into acts of obedience in order to nullify them. If he is safe from that, he instills in him self-admiration (ʿujb) and considering his deeds to be great. Among this too, he kindles in the heart the fire of envy, spite, and anger, until he leads the person to the worst deeds and most detestable states.

The treatment of his whispering is by three things. The first: frequent remembrance of God. The second: frequent seeking of refuge in God from him, and among the most beneficial things in this is reciting this surah. The third: opposing him and resolving to disobey him. If it is asked: why did He say "in the breasts of mankind" and not "in the hearts of mankind"? The answer: this indicates that the whispering does not settle firmly, and that it is not located in the heart itself, but rather hovers in the breasts around the heart.

﴿From among the jinn and mankind﴾. This explains the kind of whisperer: that it may be from the jinn, and it may be from mankind. Then, the human whisperer may mean one who whispers by deception and his wicked sayings, for he is a devil, as God, may He be exalted, says: ﴿devils of mankind and jinn﴾ [al-An'am: 112]. Or it may mean the human's own self, which commands him to evil, for it is the self that commands evil. The first is more apparent. It was also said that "from among mankind" is coordinated with "the whisperer," as if He said: I seek refuge from the evil of the whisperer, from the jinn, and from the evil of mankind, and in this view mankind are not among those who whisper. The first is more apparent and better known.

If it is asked: why did He conclude the Qur'an with the two refuge surahs (al-Mu'awwidhatayn), and what is the wisdom in that? The answer is in three aspects.

The first: our shaykh, the teacher Abu Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr, said: since the Qur'an is among the greatest blessings upon His servants, and blessings invite envy, He concluded it with what extinguishes envy, which is seeking refuge in God.

The second: it appears to me that the two refuge surahs were used to conclude it because the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said about them: "Verses have been revealed to me the like of which has never been seen." Just as he said about the opening chapter of the Book (Surat al-Fatiha): "There has not been sent down in the Torah, nor in the Gospel, nor in the Furqan, anything like it." So He opened the Qur'an with a surah like which nothing was sent down, and concluded it with two surahs the like of which has never been seen, in order to combine the excellence of the opening and the closing. Do you not see that speeches, letters, odes, and other kinds of discourse are judged by the excellence of their openings and their endings?

The third: it also appears to me that since the reader was commanded to begin his recitation by seeking refuge from the accursed Satan, the Qur'an was concluded with the two refuge surahs, so that seeking refuge in God is obtained at the beginning of the recitation and at the end of what is recited. Thus the seeking of refuge encompasses both the beginning and the end, and so that the reciter is preserved by the protection of God, in whom he sought refuge, from the start of his affair to its end. And success is from God; there is no lord but Him.

The second: it appears to me that the two refuge surahs were used to conclude it because the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said about them: "Verses have been revealed to me the like of which has never been seen." Just as he said about the opening chapter of the Book (Surat al-Fatiha): "There has not been sent down in the Torah, nor in the Gospel, nor in the Furqan, anything like it." So He opened the Qur'an with a surah like which nothing was sent down, and concluded it with two surahs the like of which has never been seen, in order to combine the excellence of the opening and the closing. Do you not see that speeches, letters, odes, and other kinds of discourse are judged by the excellence of their openings and their endings?

The third: it also appears to me that since the reader was commanded to begin his recitation by seeking refuge from the accursed Satan, the Qur'an was concluded with the two refuge surahs, so that seeking refuge in God is obtained at the beginning of the recitation and at the end of what is recited. Thus the seeking of refuge encompasses both the beginning and the end, and so that the reciter is preserved by the protection of God, in whom he sought refuge, from the start of his affair to its end. And success is from God; there is no lord but Him.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 114, verses 1–6:

﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind﴾. If it is asked: why did He attribute the Lord (rabb) specifically to mankind, when He is the Lord of everything? The answer: the seeking of refuge was from the evil of the whisperer who whispers into the breasts of people. So He singled them out for mention, because they are the ones who seek protection with this formula, and they are the intended ones here, not others. ﴿The King of mankind, the God of mankind﴾. This is ʿatf bayan (explanatory apposition). If it is asked: why did He mention His attributes in the order Lord, then King, then God? The answer: this is in ascending order of rank. The term "lord" (rabb) may be applied to many people, as one says "so-and-so is the lord of the house" and the like, so it was mentioned first because its meaning is shared. As for "king" (malik), it is applied only to a certain category of people, the kings, and there is no doubt that they are higher than the rest of people. Therefore it came after "lord." As for "God" (ilah), He is higher than the king, which is why kings do not claim to be gods. The God is only One, without partner or equal, so the attributes were concluded with Him.

If it is asked: why did he repeat the explicit mention of the genitive "mankind" in the second and third instances, rather than using a pronoun in both, given that it was mentioned earlier in "Lord of mankind"? Or why was it not enough to mention it explicitly only the second time? The answer: since it was an explanatory apposition, explicitness was appropriate there, because explanation requires clarity rather than pronouns. It was also intended to give attention to the repeated term, as in the saying of the poet:

"I see nothing outrunning death; death humbles the rich man and the poor man alike."

﴿The whisperer﴾ (al-waswas). It is derived from waswasa, which is hidden speech. It may be that al-waswas carries the meaning of al-muwaswis (the one who whispers), as if it were an active participle. This appears from the statement of Ibn ʿAtiyya: "al-waswas is among the names of Satan." It may also be a verbal noun (masdar) used to describe the whisperer for emphasis, like ʿaddal and sawwam, or it may be by omission of a noun, its meaning being "the possessor of whispering" (dhi al-waswas). Al-Zamakhshari said: the verbal noun is actually waswas with bi-l-kufr (whispering of disbelief).

﴿The sneaking one (al-khannas)﴾. Its meaning is the one who retreats on his heels and recurs occasionally. This applies fully to Satan: he whispers, and when the servant remembers God and seeks refuge in Him, he withdraws from him. Then he returns to him at a time of heedlessness from remembrance. He sneaks back in his withdrawal and then in his return after that.

﴿Who whispers into the breasts of mankind﴾. Satan's whispering into the breast of a human being takes many forms. Among them: corrupting faith and casting doubt on beliefs. If he cannot do that, he orders him to commit sins. If he cannot do that, he discourages him from acts of obedience. If he cannot do that, he introduces showing-off (riya') into acts of obedience in order to nullify them. If he is safe from that, he instills in him self-admiration (ʿujb) and considering his deeds to be great. Among this too, he kindles in the heart the fire of envy, spite, and anger, until he leads the person to the worst deeds and most detestable states.

The treatment of his whispering is by three things. The first: frequent remembrance of God. The second: frequent seeking of refuge in God from him, and among the most beneficial things in this is reciting this surah. The third: opposing him and resolving to disobey him. If it is asked: why did He say "in the breasts of mankind" and not "in the hearts of mankind"? The answer: this indicates that the whispering does not settle firmly, and that it is not located in the heart itself, but rather hovers in the breasts around the heart.

﴿From among the jinn and mankind﴾. This explains the kind of whisperer: that it may be from the jinn, and it may be from mankind. Then, the human whisperer may mean one who whispers by deception and his wicked sayings, for he is a devil, as God, may He be exalted, says: ﴿devils of mankind and jinn﴾ [al-An'am: 112]. Or it may mean the human's own self, which commands him to evil, for it is the self that commands evil. The first is more apparent. It was also said that "from among mankind" is coordinated with "the whisperer," as if He said: I seek refuge from the evil of the whisperer, from the jinn, and from the evil of mankind, and in this view mankind are not among those who whisper. The first is more apparent and better known.
